title: Robert Bly and the cult of men's inner work
gist: Today's male self-improvement podcasters like Steven Bartlett and Chris Williamson are the heirs of poet Robert Bly, whose 1990 bestseller Iron John built a 'mythopoetic' men's movement that reframed political and social problems as psychological ones to be solved by 'inner work' rather than political change.

insights.claim: Modern male self-improvement podcasters such as Steven Bartlett (Diary of a CEO) and Chris Williamson (Modern Wisdom) are the heirs of poet Robert Bly, who first monetised solving 'the crisis of masculinity' in the 1980s-90s.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: The 'men's crisis' content category is a recurring, durable market that reinvents itself each generation; useful signal for anyone tracking creator-economy and wellness verticals aimed at young men.
insights.quote: Steven Bartlett and Chris Williamson are not, however, the first gurus to gain a following from promising to solve the crisis of masculinity.

insights.claim: Contemporary 'anti-woke' male podcasters are distinguished from the manosphere by actually liking women, blending science with vibes-based 'Bro-Science' in a Joe Rogan tone minus the conspiracy content.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Segmenting the male-audience media market by its stance toward women clarifies which brands are advertiser-safe versus toxic.

insights.claim: Robert Bly located the origin of the masculinity crisis in the Industrial Revolution, when fathers left the home for factories and sons, raised by mothers, lost the male-only initiation that made boys into men.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: A template narrative that recurs in today's discourse: blaming modern male malaise on lost pre-industrial male spaces rather than on economic or policy factors.
insights.quote: Men had lost access to the male-only spaces that had provided the necessary initiation which made boys into men.
insights.locator: In the 1980s and 1990s, the poet Robert Bly

insights.claim: Bly's 1990 book Iron John: A Book About Men topped the New York Times bestseller list for 62 weeks and became the spiritual manual of the American men's movement.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of the commercial scale a single masculinity title can reach, a benchmark for the genre's ceiling.
insights.quote: which was at the top of the New York Times bestseller list for 62 weeks
insights.locator: Bly told this story in his 1990 book

insights.claim: A 90-minute Bill Moyers television segment in 1990 turned a scattered miscellany of men's gatherings into a nationally recognised 'men's movement', showing the catalytic role of a single mass-media appearance.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Illustrates how one legacy-media placement can convert a niche subculture into a mainstream movement, still relevant to how creator brands scale.
insights.quote: After a 90-minute segment with Bill Moyers in 1990, Bly became a household name
insights.locator: This narrative animated the men's conferences

insights.claim: Bly's core move was to recast political problems as personal psychology, arguing the world's problems were best solved by 'inner work' rather than political change.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: This depoliticisation-as-therapy frame is the through-line to modern self-optimisation culture and its appeal to disengaged audiences.
insights.quote: The world's problems as well as those of men and women were best solved by inner work rather than political change.
insights.locator: By and large, feminism was considered

insights.claim: Bly defined his ideal masculinity against two archetypes he blamed for modern ills: the aggressive 'fifties man' (responsible for Vietnam and rapacious executives) and the soft, unhappy 'seventies man'.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: A durable rhetorical structure: contrast archetypes to sell a 'third way' identity, echoed by later figures who market a middle path between toxic and passive masculinity.
insights.locator: Bly defined his ideal masculinity against two other male archetypes

insights.claim: The author draws a direct line from Bly's 'inner work' ethos to Jordan Peterson's 'make your bed' advice: fix your own house before trying to change the world.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Positions Peterson within a decades-old lineage rather than as a novel phenomenon, useful context for anyone assessing the self-help influencer space.
insights.quote: Like Jordan Peterson's 'make your bed', there was no need to change the world until your own house was in order.
insights.locator: Bly was a master and pioneer in Bro-Science

insights.claim: Sociologist Michael Schwalbe's field study found the mythopoetic men's movement drew a narrow demographic: former 1960s activists who worked in female-dominated workplaces, married feminist women, and mostly opposed the Gulf War despite broad public support for it.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: A reminder that a bestseller's mass reach does not equal a broad participant base; movements often mobilise a self-selecting sliver.
insights.quote: only a very particular segment of society was drawn to the groups and retreats
insights.locator: Michael Schwalbe, a sociologist who conducted a field study

insights.claim: The movement's participants were 'seventies men' seeking escape from what they felt was the 'overwhelming female energy' of everyday life, feeling uniquely vulnerable to accusations of sexism because of their closeness to feminist women.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: Shows the emotional demand driving the product: retreat and belonging, not ideology, a consumer insight relevant to today's men's wellness offerings.
insights.quote: the forest retreats provided an escape from the 'overwhelming female energy' of everyday life
insights.locator: These men saw themselves in Bly's soft 'seventies man'

insights.claim: Bly's movement was contradictory: it longed for pre-industrial times and railed against modernity yet was itself a distinctly modern therapeutic movement built on conferences and retreats.
insights.speaker: Felice Basbøll
insights.so_what: The nostalgia-vs-modernity tension is a recurring feature of wellness and identity brands that sell 'ancient wisdom' through modern commercial formats.
insights.quote: Bly might have longed for pre-industrial times, but his was a distinctly modern movement.
insights.locator: Bly himself had been on a personal journey
